title: Sangrand at home
hook: marking the new month with a reading
tomorrow: a year of gurpurabs, lived. what's left to plan?

segments.voice: Yesterday, freedom for all: a Guru who stood for someone else's right to pray, and a hall of mixed chairs. Now the calendar flips, and some homes mark it with a reading.

A new month usually means a new bill, a fresh page on the wall calendar, a reminder to change the air filter. Here's something odd in the Granth. Guru Arjan wrote a song of the months, the Barah Maha, with a stanza for each month in turn. Then, near the end, he says no month is special in itself. So why would anyone keep a reading for the first day of the month?
screen: `A NEW BILL, A FRESH PAGE.` → `A SONG WITH A STANZA PER MONTH.` → `THEN: NO MONTH IS SPECIAL?`

segments.voice: The day is Sangrand, when the sun moves into a new sign and the Punjabi solar month begins. On it, some gurdwaras and some homes read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha, so the month opens with its own verse. Each stanza turns a season toward the soul. In Chet, it says, remembering the Lord brings deep joy. In Vaisakh, it asks how anyone parted from love can be patient. Now the puzzle. Near the close, on Ang one thirty-six, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: the months, the days, the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord's glance of grace falls. So the date isn't magic. What makes a day good is remembering in it. Sikhs live that out two ways. Some love Sangrand as a doorway: a set time to begin the month with its verse, at home or in sangat. Others prefer not to treat any date as holier than another, and say every day is the same before God. Both lean on the same line, and both agree on what it asks: whatever the date, begin it remembering. That's what a reading at home on Sangrand does. It opens a month with a line instead of a to-do list.
screen: `SANGRAND: THE MONTH BEGINS.` · `A STANZA FOR EACH MONTH.` · `BLESSED WHERE GRACE FALLS.` · `A DOORWAY, OR EVERY DAY ALIKE.` · then, large: `A NEW MONTH.`

segments.voice: Find this month's stanza, in a gutka, an app or a printed Barah Maha, or choose any line of Gurbani you know. Copy one line by hand, slowly, in whatever script you can. Then rest your eyes on what you wrote, and breathe with it until the sit ends.

howItsDone: On Sangrand, the first day of the Punjabi solar month, some gurdwaras hold a special diwan where the month's stanza of the Barah Maha (Majh, Guru Arjan) is read; some families read it at home, while other Sikhs keep no special observance for the date.

options: Worth it. No date is magic, but a line at breakfast helps you begin the month remembering.
Skip it. Guru Arjan says no month is special, so a Sangrand reading is pointless.
Only at the gurdwara. A Sangrand reading counts when the whole sangat hears it.
chat.meaning: The Barah Maha says days are blessed where grace falls. A reading on Sangrand doesn't make the date holy; it helps you begin it remembering.
